title: LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation
mission: Regulate competitive transport of large neutral amino acids across the blood–brain barrier in response to circulating substrate availability.
summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) helps control which amino acids can enter the brain. Tyrosine, tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) compete for this shared route. Human feeding experiments show that meal composition and protein source can alter their relative availability in blood. The response depends on the tested meal and sampling period, rather than a universal carbohydrate-to-protein rule. This transport step connects circulating precursor supply with downstream neurotransmitter pathways.
key_constraints: BRS1(KC1) - Amino Acid Quality & Competitive Balance
dose_sensitivity: Pattern target rather than single nutrient threshold; depends on protein/carbohydrate composition
scientific_findings_intro: LAT1 transport identity is separated from the experimental finding that meal composition changes plasma precursor ratios. Breakfast, evening-meal and protein-source results show why a between-meal difference must not be described as a universal rise above baseline. Plasma ratios do not directly measure brain transport or neurotransmitter production. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

dietary_lever_presentations.label: Meal carbohydrate-to-protein composition
dietary_lever_presentations.reader_description: The carbohydrate-to-protein composition of the tested breakfasts changed blood ratios among amino acids competing for brain entry. A between-meal contrast is not necessarily an increase above baseline: the recovered breakfast study found lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after its protein-rich meal. Responses differ with meal context and protein source. No best ratio or improvement in brain function is established.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Meal-level LNAA competition at LAT1 can shift plasma tyrosine and tryptophan ratios and, on review evidence, brain-entry bias {{cite:fernstrom_lnna_2013,ashley_breakfast_1985,wurtman_effects_2003}}. The attached meal studies do not measure attention or ADHD outcomes, and transport modulation cannot substitute for substrate sufficiency or downstream signalling.

The tested meals changed competitive plasma ratios; the recovered breakfast study did not show a tyrosine-ratio rise after protein {{cite:wurtman_effects_2003}}. This remains a translational mapping, not demonstrated motivation, drive or ADHD benefit.

Carbohydrate-rich versus protein-rich meals can change the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio {{cite:wurtman_effects_2003,ashley_breakfast_1985,fernstrom_lnna_2013}}. Plasma-ratio change is not serotonin signalling or an emotional-regulation benefit.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Shared LAT1 transport and precursor competition
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) carries competing amino acids as part of an exchanger complex. Blood ratios describe substrate presentation, not measured transport flux.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This establishes competitive transport biology. It does not show that eating more tyrosine or tryptophan increases brain monoamines or improves function.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Large neutral amino acids share competitive transport through LAT1 (SLC7A5) with the SLC3A2 heavy chain; plasma composition helps shape substrate availability but is not a direct measurement of net brain uptake.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Rat tracer experiments establish saturable BBB amino-acid uptake and competitive inhibition of tryptophan entry. Molecular expression experiments identify LAT1 substrate selectivity and 4F2hc-dependent function; bovine brain-capillary cloning connects that molecular system to the BBB, and human complex structures support its architecture. These are convergent experimental levels, not interchangeable human meal trials or independent replications of one protocol. The existing competitive-transport proposition is retained; human plasma observations remain in SF2 and central-compartment observations qualify SF3.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The early rat experiments predate molecular identification and do not alone identify SLC7A5. Heterologous transport and human protein structures do not quantify intact human BBB flux after meals. Exchange substrates, affinity, membrane context and other determinants qualify plasma-ratio predictions. Pardridge 1975/1977 and Yan 2019 were checked at abstract/record level here; no full-method appraisal is claimed. The pinned SEC v2 predates this consolidation and remains unchanged; separate versioned appraisal is required before assigning confidence to the expanded evidence base.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary and plasma LNAA ratios influence LAT1-mediated brain uptake of tyrosine, tryptophan and related amino acids and can change precursor availability for neurotransmitter synthesis.

assessment.study: Narrative review of dietary LNAA effects on brain transport and neurochemistry.
assessment.population: Mixed human and experimental literature; not a single intervention sample.
assessment.result: Identified competitive LAT1 transport and plasma-ratio dependence as determinants of brain LNAA entry.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes the shared-transporter rule that defines this PM.
assessment.limitations: Review synthesis; does not by itself demonstrate that ordinary meals change human brain monoamines or function.

evidence_considered.label: Pardridge & Oldendorf (1975)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tracer uptake was saturable with added unlabelled amino acid, supporting carrier-mediated BBB transport.

assessment.study: Kinetic analysis of blood-brain barrier transport of amino acids
assessment.population: Anesthetized rats; carotid radiolabelled amino-acid injection and tissue sampling at 15 seconds.
assessment.result: Tracer uptake was saturable with added unlabelled amino acid, supporting carrier-mediated BBB transport.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect across distinct experimental models.
assessment.evidence_summary: Tracer uptake was saturable with added unlabelled amino acid, supporting carrier-mediated BBB transport.
assessment.limitations: PubMed abstract inspected. Fourteen amino acids span more than the LAT1 substrate class; not molecular identification or human dietary flux.

evidence_considered.label: Pardridge (1977)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Cross-inhibition and self-inhibition constants were consistent with competition at a shared transport site.

assessment.study: Kinetics of competitive inhibition of neutral amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier
assessment.population: Barbiturate-anesthetized rats; single-injection radiolabelled tryptophan uptake with neutral amino-acid competitors.
assessment.result: Cross-inhibition and self-inhibition constants were consistent with competition at a shared transport site.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect across distinct experimental models.
assessment.evidence_summary: Cross-inhibition and self-inhibition constants were consistent with competition at a shared transport site.
assessment.limitations: Scite abstract fallback only. Predicted influx from kinetic equations is distinct from a measured human meal effect; same investigator lineage as the 1975 study.

evidence_considered.label: Kanai et al. (1998)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Co-expression enabled saturable sodium-independent LNAA transport; extracellular leucine stimulated efflux of preloaded leucine, supporting exchange.

assessment.study: Expression cloning and characterization of a transporter for large neutral amino acids activated by the heavy chain of 4F2 antigen (CD98)
assessment.population: Rat C6 glioma cDNA expressed in Xenopus oocytes with 4F2hc; radiotracer uptake, competition and efflux assays.
assessment.result: Co-expression enabled saturable sodium-independent LNAA transport; extracellular leucine stimulated efflux of preloaded leucine, supporting exchange.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect across distinct experimental models.
assessment.evidence_summary: Co-expression enabled saturable sodium-independent LNAA transport; extracellular leucine stimulated efflux of preloaded leucine, supporting exchange.
assessment.limitations: Scite full-text methods and results inspected. Heterologous rat transporter assay, not human BBB flux; substrate selectivity does not establish dietary efficacy.

evidence_considered.label: Boado et al. (1999)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Brain-capillary-derived LAT1 supported sodium-independent tryptophan uptake inhibited by large neutral amino acids, linking molecular transport properties to BBB-derived material.

assessment.study: Selective expression of the large neutral amino acid transporter at the blood-brain barrier
assessment.population: Bovine brain-capillary cDNA and RNA analysis; Xenopus oocytes co-expressing bovine LAT1 and rat 4F2hc.
assessment.result: Brain-capillary-derived LAT1 supported sodium-independent tryptophan uptake inhibited by large neutral amino acids, linking molecular transport properties to BBB-derived material.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect across distinct experimental models.
assessment.evidence_summary: Brain-capillary-derived LAT1 supported sodium-independent tryptophan uptake inhibited by large neutral amino acids, linking molecular transport properties to BBB-derived material.
assessment.limitations: Scite full-text methods and relevant results inspected. Bovine tissue and heterologous assay, not a human intervention; Pardridge is a coauthor, so independence is not inferred from publication count.

evidence_considered.label: Yan et al. (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human LAT1–4F2hc structures support heteromeric architecture, including an inhibitor-bound state.

assessment.study: Structure of the human LAT1–4F2hc heteromeric amino acid transporter complex
assessment.population: Human protein-complex cryo-electron microscopy; published abstract and associated structural record.
assessment.result: Human LAT1–4F2hc structures support heteromeric architecture, including an inhibitor-bound state.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled effect across distinct experimental models.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human LAT1–4F2hc structures support heteromeric architecture, including an inhibitor-bound state.
assessment.limitations: Publisher abstract/structural record only; Scite supplied no readable text. Human protein is not human clinical evidence or measured BBB flux.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Meal composition and protein source alter plasma precursor ratios
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human feeding experiments demonstrate context-dependent plasma-ratio changes. A higher ratio after one meal than another is not necessarily an increase above baseline.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Retain the admitted meal-composition regulatory relationship at its plasma-ratio ceiling. Protein-source experiments qualify generalisation; they do not establish a best ratio, an additional nutrient requirement or a clinical protocol.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In the studied healthy adults, meal composition and tested protein sources can alter plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids; the direction and tyrosine response depend on the exposure and sampling context, without establishing increased human brain transport or neurotransmitter synthesis.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Breakfast contrasts and separate protein-source experiments support meal-responsive precursor ratios, but not one universal direction. The recovered Wurtman table shows lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after the protein-rich breakfast, not an increased tyrosine ratio. Evening-meal null results and a starch-control null constrain extrapolation. Brain uptake and downstream effects were not measured by those plasma experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Small acute healthy-adult samples; different meals, ratio denominators and sampling windows; incomplete historical methods retrieval. No population-wide optimum or direct human brain-flux estimate. Evening null results limit generalisation but are not equivalence evidence.

evidence_considered.label: Ashley et al. (1985)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Breakfast carbohydrate-versus-protein composition changed the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio in healthy lean young men.

assessment.study: Controlled breakfast-composition experiment measuring plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids.
assessment.result: Breakfast composition altered the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Directional meal contrast; no general clinical effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows that a single ordinary breakfast can move the tryptophan competitive ratio.
assessment.limitations: Plasma ratio only; no brain transport, serotonin or functional measure; young male sample.

evidence_considered.label: Wurtman et al. (2003)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.

assessment.study: Random-order two-breakfast crossover; sampling through four hours, chromatographic amino-acid assays and mixed-model analysis with order and multiplicity considered.
assessment.population: Nine young adults entered; eight completed both conditions (six women, two men).
assessment.result: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Median between-breakfast contrast: 54% for tryptophan ratio and 28% for tyrosine ratio; these are not increases after protein. Carbohydrate-arm increases from baseline were not significant.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct plasma contrast, not brain transport.
assessment.limitations: One incomplete participant; visible meal differences and unreported concealment/assay blinding; residual uncertainty in magnitude and generalisation.

evidence_considered.label: Ashley et al. (1982)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.

assessment.study: Within-person evening meal comparison; author-posted results and figures recovered.
assessment.result: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.
assessment.effect_magnitude: See source-specific results; no pooled effect or invented confidence interval.
assessment.evidence_summary: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.
assessment.limitations: Different meals and time window from breakfast experiments; null significance does not establish equivalence.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom et al. (2013), protein-source experiment
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.

assessment.study: Four-visit feeding experiment, four-hour chromatographic sampling; full institutional manuscript examined.
assessment.result: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.
assessment.effect_magnitude: See source-specific results; no pooled effect or invented confidence interval.
assessment.evidence_summary: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.
assessment.limitations: Order randomisation and blinding not established in the examined report; different denominator from Wurtman. Not a universal food ranking.

evidence_dependency: Ashley breakfast and evening reports share investigators; do not count them as independent-team replication. Wurtman breakfast and Fernstrom protein-source experiments are distinct datasets and teams, but test different protocols. Ratio denominators differ; no pooled effect is calculated. Markus protein studies are contextual corroboration, not extra replications of a carbohydrate-to-protein protocol.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma-ratio changes do not establish ordinary-meal functional benefit
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Enriched-protein studies include functional endpoints, but their exposures and populations differ from ordinary meals. Keep that evidence distinct from a demonstrated LAT1-mediated clinical effect.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Phenome mappings remain translational relationships. Precursor-loading or depletion cognition literature is a different exposure and must not be read as ordinary-meal LAT1 evidence.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The ordinary-meal studies assessed here measured plasma amino-acid ratios, not brain transport or ADHD outcomes; findings from enriched-protein attention studies do not establish ordinary-meal efficacy.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The original meal studies do not measure functional outcomes. Markus et al. (2005) measured morning attention after an enriched-protein protocol, while a newer athlete trial reported null sleep/performance results. These contexts cannot validate a general ordinary-meal benefit or prove mediation by LAT1. Teff (1989) provides a separate patient-CSF observation: protein-associated tyrosine elevation with null tryptophan and amine-metabolite responses. CSF concentration is not LAT1 flux or neurotransmitter synthesis; the unexplained carbohydrate-associated MHPG rise is retained without causal interpretation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is an assessment-scope boundary, not a claim that functional evidence is absent from the entire literature. The enriched-protein trials are not ordinary-meal or ADHD trials; no equivalence or mediation is inferred.

evidence_considered.label: Aquili (2020)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tryptophan and tyrosine can modulate executive function and reward processing in reviewed experimental designs, largely through acute depletion or loading rather than ordinary meals.

assessment.study: Narrative review of tryptophan and tyrosine in executive function and reward processing.
assessment.population: Mixed experimental and clinical literature; not an ordinary-meal LAT1 sample.
assessment.result: Precursor availability was linked to executive and reward measures in depletion and loading contexts.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled ordinary-meal or ADHD effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows that precursor-manipulation studies exist, but they are the wrong construct for this PM’s meal-level LAT1 claim.
assessment.limitations: Review-level; depletion and loading are not carbohydrate–protein meals and do not measure LAT1 transport.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Ashley et al. (1985)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Demonstrates that breakfast composition changes the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: No attention, emotional-regulation or ADHD outcome was measured.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Wurtman et al. (2003)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Demonstrates that ordinary high-carbohydrate and high-protein meals move plasma tryptophan and tyrosine ratios.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Plasma ratios are not Phenome or clinical endpoints.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Fernstrom (2013)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Frames why plasma LNAA ratios can change brain precursor entry.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Review of transport and neurochemistry, not a meal-to-Phenome or ADHD trial.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Teff et al. (1989)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Central-compartment precursor observation complements peripheral meal measurements.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: CSF concentration is not LAT1 flux, neurotransmitter synthesis or a functional outcome; not primary evidence for the functional-benefit proposition.
connected_supportive_evidence.directional_finding: In patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus, a protein breakfast raised CSF tyrosine but not tryptophan or measured amine metabolites; the carbohydrate condition raised MHPG but not the other reported precursors/metabolites.

assessment.study: Breakfast/water comparisons with lumbar CSF sampling 2.5 hours later during one week.
assessment.population: Patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus; sample size and full methods not verified from accessible abstract.
assessment.result: Protein-associated CSF tyrosine response with null tryptophan and amine-metabolite observations; carbohydrate-associated MHPG rise was unexplained.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No verified numerical magnitude or equivalence estimate extracted.
assessment.evidence_summary: Central-compartment concentration evidence, not direct LAT1 transport flux or synthesis.
assessment.limitations: Scite abstract fallback only. Patient population, lumbar compartment and sampling time limit generalisation; no causal LAT1 mediation, cognition or ADHD benefit established.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma LNAA ratios are not monoamine dosing
scientific_findings.finding_summary: A change in the plasma tryptophan or tyrosine ratio is not a measurement of brain LAT1 flux, neurotransmitter synthesis or a functional outcome.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Read meal studies as plasma competitive-balance evidence. Do not restate them as serotonin, dopamine or ADHD effects.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Plasma large-neutral-amino-acid ratio change after a meal is not equivalent to measured brain transport, monoamine synthesis or a Phenome outcome.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human meal papers report circulating amino-acid ratios. The transport review explains why those ratios matter at LAT1. Neither layer substitutes for a brain-transport, synthesis-flux or outcome measure.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The constraint is interpretive. It does not deny that brain entry can follow plasma ratios; it denies treating the attached meal endpoints as if they were those later steps.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary LNAA patterns can change brain precursor availability, but plasma ratio, brain uptake and neurotransmitter synthesis are separable steps.

assessment.study: Narrative review distinguishing plasma LNAA ratios, LAT1 transport and downstream neurochemistry.
assessment.result: Supported competitive transport while keeping later neurochemical steps distinct.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supplies the interpretive boundary between ratio change and monoamine effect.
assessment.limitations: Review-level; does not replace a human brain-transport experiment.

evidence_dependency: Fernstrom (2013) is also primary Evidence Considered in PM2-F1. Reuse here is interpretive, not an independent replication of the transport rule.

decision.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the shared indispensable-amino-acid quality pool can constrain this mechanism’s governed LAT1 competitive-transport capacity.
established_links: DIAAS and related scores measure digestible IAA adequacy for protein quality (FAO 2013; Mariotti 2019).
LAT1 competition depends on the relative plasma LNAA mix (Fernstrom 2013).
inferred_links: Incomplete IAA quality would therefore change the LNAA mix and constrain transport capacity.
decision.rationale: Assessment was completed. Quality-scoring evidence does not measure LAT1 competition. Fernstrom’s competitive effects assume LNAAs are present; they do not show that a DIAAS-type quality shortfall constrains transport capacity. Ownership on PM1 does not decide this arm.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Superseded scope: this proposition concerns the former broad indispensable-amino-acid quality arm. Current BRS1 KC1 is the monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive pool. Archiving does not reject general protein-quality biology or alter the separately assessed competitive/supply decisions.

decision.applicability_proposition: This mechanism governs meal-level LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance.
established_links: Meal-level LNAA competition at LAT1 is the state this PM governs (PM2-F1, PM2-F2).
decision.rationale: Type D is met in the governs mode. This does not decide the quality arm.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Metadata migration only: preserve the established governs/constrained-by interpretation as a typed Conditional constraint for FM summary derivation. No stronger scientific admission.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Dominant
evidence_qualification.rationale: Retain the accepted dietary state-regulation relationship, qualified to measured plasma-ratio effects.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: Acute plasma-ratio modulation in studied healthy adults, not demonstrated optimisation of human brain transport or function.

routes.intervention_effect: Tested meal composition alters plasma competitive precursor ratios.
routes.limitations: Context-dependent responses, including null contrasts; no optimum or clinical benefit.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Retain Dietary Requirements as the existing admitted regulatory-state route, not a new capacity requirement. No SOP or lifestyle candidate independently establishes a preferred transport-optimisation protocol in this bounded assessment.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: No head-to-head superiority over all SOP or lifestyle routes; changes in plasma ratios are not automatically beneficial.

assessments.relevance: Regulates the measured competitive precursor presentation state.
assessments.directness: Plasma endpoint is directly measured; brain transport remains inferred.
assessments.extent: Different acute meals and proteins give different responses; no universal direction or dose target.
